title: Treasure in the Name
hook: the Name is a treasure found within, not in markets (Anand)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the devotees' path, and your line, the narrow way. Did you manage fewer words in one conversation? Today, the thing those devotees find on the way. Day three hundred ninety-one.

There's an old story told all over India about a musk deer. A sweet, wonderful scent follows it everywhere, and it drives the deer wild. It runs through forests, over hills, nose to every flower and bush, desperate to find where the smell is coming from. It never does. Because the scent is coming from the deer itself. The musk is in its own body. It has been carrying the treasure the whole time it's been searching. Sikh teachers love that story, and so does Anand Sahib's theme for today. Today: treasure in the Name.
screen: `A MUSK DEER CHASING A SCENT.` → `OVER HILLS, THROUGH FORESTS.` → `THE SCENT WAS ITS OWN.`

segments.voice: Anand Sahib, like much of gurbani, speaks of the Name as a treasure, one that can't be found in markets or bought with money, and, as you heard on day three hundred eighty-eight, can't be won by cleverness either. It's found within, through the Guru. That idea runs right through the Guru Granth Sahib. The Bhagat Pipa, one of the saints whose words sit in the Granth beside the Gurus, put it in a line Sikhs often quote. In paraphrase: whatever is in the universe is also in the body, and whoever searches, finds it. So the treasure isn't hidden somewhere far away. It's hidden close. Which is precisely why it's hard to find. We look outward by habit. Markets, achievements, other people's approval, the next place, the next thing. Like the deer, we're nose-down in every bush but our own. Now, a careful note. Sikhs don't say the outer world is worthless. The Gurus lived in it fully: farming, trading, raising families, building towns. Work and markets aren't the enemy. The point is about where the treasure is kept. You can work at the market all day. You just won't find the Name for sale there. And how do you look within? The Sikh answer is simple and steady: simran, remembering the Name; the shabad, the Guru's Word; and the company of others on the same path, the sangat. These are like a lamp turned inward. Over the last few days, Anand has said the Name is the support, the bliss known through the Guru, a gift given, not grabbed, not found by cleverness, the Word that clears doubt, the narrow way. Today it adds one more picture. It's treasure. And it's been yours to find the whole time.
screen: `A TREASURE NOT FOR SALE.` · `WHAT'S IN THE UNIVERSE IS IN THE BODY.` · `WORK AND MARKETS AREN'T THE ENEMY.` · `SIMRAN, SHABAD, SANGAT: A LAMP INWARD.` · then, large: `TREASURE WITHIN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look inward for one minute. Close your eyes, or lower them. Breathe slowly. Instead of following your thoughts outward, to the day's plans and people, turn your attention around, gently, toward the place the attention is coming from. Notice the breath. Notice the stillness under the thoughts. Don't try to find anything. Just look in, the way you'd look into a quiet room. If you pray, you can say Waheguru softly and let it lead you in. If you don't, just rest in the looking. The bell holds the time.
Treasure in the Name. Anand's picture of the Name as a treasure found within, through the Guru, not bought in any market, like the musk deer's own scent.
Your line: treasure within. Today, when you catch yourself searching outside for something to make you feel complete, stop for one breath and look in first. Day three hundred ninety-one.

howItsDone: Many Sikhs understand the Name as a treasure found within through simran, the Guru's Word and the sangat, a theme that runs through Anand Sahib and the whole Guru Granth Sahib.

fork.setup: you're the musk deer, running from hill to hill after a wonderful scent you can never find. what's the answer the story gives?
options: the scent is your own: the treasure is within.
give up on the scent entirely.
fork.reveal: the musk was in the deer's own body the whole time. Sikh teachers use the story for the Name: a treasure found within, through the Guru.

original.note: Gurmukhi: nidhaan, treasure; gurbani often calls the Name a treasure found within.

trapdoor: what you thought: a line about spiritual riches somewhere above.
what it means: the Name is a treasure already within, found through the Guru, simran and the sangat, not bought or won.
what a scholar hears: Bhagat Pipa's line 'jo brahmande soee pinde', what is in the cosmos is in the body, at Ang 695, gives the Granth's classic statement of the treasure within.

sources.ref: Anand Sahib, Ang 917–922 (the Name as treasure within)
Bhagat Pipa, Raag Dhanasari, Ang 695 ('jo brahmande soee pinde, jo khojai so paavai')
